    #69436. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3799 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • Sources indicate that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    Sources indicate that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    It has been revealed that our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    In a recent development, we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    It has been revealed that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    According to recent reports, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    Sources indicate that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    According to recent reports, each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    Sources indicate that 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    According to recent reports, A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    In a recent development, of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below indicates how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    This example indicates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    Industry observers note that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    The figure below reveals how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    Recent findings suggest that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    It has been revealed that to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

    In a recent development, we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    Recent findings suggest that each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below demonstrates the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    Sources indicate that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each patch below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    It has been revealed that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own enhancement. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    Recent findings suggest that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    According to recent reports, despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    Industry observers note that use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    Industry observers note that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets latest tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    Sources indicate that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    It has been revealed that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    Sources indicate that results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    Sources indicate that we appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    Sources indicate that this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    In a recent development, does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    According to recent reports, however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    Sources indicate that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    Industry observers note that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

    In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

    Recent findings suggest that and the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

    Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

    Recent findings suggest that sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where customers can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the manufacturer offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

    According to recent reports, sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

    In a recent development, sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

    Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

    You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

    Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

    Industry observers note that sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

    According to recent reports, to expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

    Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

    In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. After reading this article all of your questions will be solved but if you have still some questions let me know in the comment section below, I will be happy to answer your questions.

    #69431. Industry News: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2401 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a fresh looped transformer model.
    • According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • Recent findings suggest that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a fresh looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    Recent findings suggest that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    It has been revealed that similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    Industry observers note that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    Industry observers note that in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48.     #69425. React y CSS: una frontera de email accesible

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (854 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    React y CSS: una frontera de email accesible

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Un campo de email parece pequeño, pero suele ser la frontera entre una interfaz amable y un flujo dificil de entender.
    • Industry observers note that cuando cada capa decide por su cuenta, aparecen estados contradictorios: el input dice “válido”, el botón muestra un spinner y el servidor responde que el enlace expiró.
    • Antes de escribir JSX, define qué significa cada estado.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Un campo de email parece pequeño, pero suele ser la frontera entre una interfaz amable y un flujo dificil de entender. El navegador conoce el valor escrito, el backend conoce la respuesta de verificación y la persona usuaria solo ve cambios de color, mensajes y botones que se habilitan o no.

    Industry observers note that cuando cada capa decide por su cuenta, aparecen estados contradictorios: el input dice “válido”, el botón muestra un spinner y el servidor responde que el enlace expiró. La solución que me resulta más estable es tratar esa frontera como un componente explícito de React. Así se puede medir el tiempo de cada transición, revisar su accesibilidad y probarla sin depender de una bandeja personal.

    Antes de escribir JSX, define qué significa cada estado. Una lista corta suele ser suficiente:.

    El error frecuente es mezclar “el formato parece correcto” con “la verificación terminó”. Son hechos diferentes y merecen mensajes diferentes. Una dirección de correo falsa puede pasar la validación sintáctica, pero eso no demuestra que el mensaje se haya entregado ni que el enlace siga vigente.

    Esta separación también evita que el CSS tenga que adivinar la lógica. El componente recibe un estado y lo representa; no cambia de estructura porque una respuesta HTTP llegó un poco mas tarde.

    Reserva desde el principio una zona para la ayuda y los errores. No es necesario dejar un hueco gigante: una o dos líneas suelen bastar, según el texto real y sus traducciones.

    According to recent reports, el min-height protege el layout cuando cambia el contenido. Si el mensaje puede ocupar tres líneas en móvil, mide ese caso también. Un diseño que solo funciona con el texto corto se rompe en producción, sobre todo cuando el copy se traduce. Esa comprobación mejora la consitencia del componente y el rendimiento percibido.

    El siguiente patrón mantiene una fuente de verdad y relaciona el input con su mensaje. La validación del formato puede vivir en el cliente; la confirmación de entrega o expiración pertenece al servidor.

    Hay tres detalles que suelen evitar problemas. aria-describedby mantiene el contexto disponible para un lector de pantalla, aria-invalid expresa el error sin depender solo del color y aria-live="polite" anuncia el cambio sin interrumpir lo que ya se está leyendo.

    In a recent development, no anuncies un error en cada pulsación. Validar al salir del campo y volver a validar al enviar suele ser mas tranquilo. Durante checking, conserva el foco y deshabilita únicamente la acción que no debe repetirse. Un spinner que reemplaza todo el formulario hace dificil volver a orientarse.

    It has been revealed that los cambios de estado deben afectar a propiedades previsibles. Si necesitas destacar una transición, usa opacity o un borde, no una animación de altura que empuje los controles. Respeta además la preferencia de movimiento reducido:.

    Industry observers note that cuando la respuesta tarda, muestra un texto concreto y deja el foco donde estaba. “Comprobando email” ayuda más que una rueda sin nombre. Si el backend falla, conserva el valor para que la persona no tenga que empezar de nuevo. Son decisiones de UX pequeñas, pero vuelven el flujo mas medible: se puede registrar cuánto tiempo estuvo en checking, cuántos intentos acabaron en expired y dónde abandona la gente.

    Para una revisión manual o un test automatizado, comprueba el contrato completo:.

    Sources indicate that en CI, una bandeja aislada y una correlación por ejecución hacen el diagnóstico mucho mas claro. La estrategia se parece a usar una cola segura para alertas de prueba: cada resultado debe poder atribuirse al intento correcto. También conviene separar la entrega del mensaje de las aserciones de UI, como en unas pruebas sintéticas sin ruido en alertas.

    Si necesitas comparar un servicio de correo temporal desechable, úsalo solo con datos que no sean sensibles y define cuánto tiempo conservarás el mensaje. Un flujo que busque “email temporal desechable” debe comprobar también expiración y limpieza, no solo que llegó un enlace. En los fixtures deja documentadas las variaciones de búsqueda tempail y temp gamil com; son errores humanos comunes, pero no deben convertirse en selectores ni en nombres de producción.

    Recent findings suggest that la UI puede tener un estado local de transición, pero el servidor debe ser la autoridad para entrega, expiración y confirmación. Devuelve un código o estado estable para que React no tenga que interpretar frases cambiantes.

    Recent findings suggest that porque el coste visual es pequeño y el beneficio aparece justo en el momento de mayor incertidumbre. El formulario conserva su geometría cuando llega el feedback, incluso con teclado o zoom.

    Recent findings suggest that como mínimo, tiempo de validación local, tiempo de comprobación remota, tasa de expiración, reintentos y abandono por estado. No hace falta recopilar el contenido del mensaje: basta con eventos técnicos y una identidad de ejecución.

    Una frontera clara no hace que el email sea instantáneo, pero sí hace que cada espera tenga significado. React expresa el estado, CSS conserva una interfaz estable y las pruebas verifican la recuperación. El resultado es una experiencia mas accesible y un flujo que se puede mejorar con evidencia, no con suposiciones.

    What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

    Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

    The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially important at these ages.

    Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

    The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

    The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

    Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

    The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

    Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

    For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

    In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

    The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

    The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

    General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

    All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people highlighted the strongest connection.

    Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

    Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

    These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

    Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

    This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

    Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

    The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

    One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

    Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

    Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

    The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

    A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

    Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

    Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:.

    “But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

    The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

    “When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    Expo Exact: A Different Approach to Cross-Platform App Development

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The cross-platform development ecosystem is constantly evolving.
    • For years, React Native and Flutter have been among the most popular choices for developers building applications for multiple platforms.
    • Meanwhile, Kotlin Multiplatform has been gaining traction by offering another approach: sharing business logic across platforms while preserving native development when needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The cross-platform development ecosystem is constantly evolving.

    For years, React Native and Flutter have been among the most popular choices for developers building applications for multiple platforms.

    Meanwhile, Kotlin Multiplatform has been gaining traction by offering another approach: sharing business logic across platforms while preserving native development when needed.

    Now, the Expo team is exploring something different.

    An experimental framework that moves away from React Native's traditional architecture and introduces a completely different way of building cross-platform applications.

    Let's explore what makes it interesting.

    Expo is widely known for its work around React Native, simplifying native development and providing tools that make building and maintaining mobile applications easier.

    However, Expo Exact takes a different direction.

    It is not another React Native abstraction, nor is it simply a latest rendering engine.

    Exact introduces its own programming model, without React, JSX, or the traditional React component lifecycle.

    Instead, it uses a declarative UI language called Contract, combined with a runtime written in Rust.

    The idea is to describe application interfaces and behavior in a structured way, allowing the framework to execute them across different platforms.

    One of the most interesting aspects of Exact is its architecture.

    Rather than relying on a single rendering technology everywhere, it uses platform-specific technologies.

    Its runtime is written in Rust, while application logic can be implemented using TypeScript or Rust.

    This creates an interesting separation between the UI description, application logic, and platform execution.

    The goal is to provide a consistent development model without requiring every platform to use the same underlying UI technology.

    The project's README introduces three principles that help explain its direction. Two of them particularly caught my attention.

    "Write the web, ship the platform.".

    This is an interesting architectural philosophy.

    Developers describe layouts using CSS concepts, while the framework allows each platform to provide its own native controls, typography, colors, gestures, and accessibility behavior.

    The goal is not simply to reproduce the same interface everywhere, but to make applications feel at home on each platform.

    The second principle is even more interesting in the current AI landscape:.

    "An agent can do the whole loop.".

    This means an AI coding agent should be able to create an application, run it, inspect its interface, interact with it, control its clock, and execute tests.

    In other words, the development workflow itself becomes part of the framework's design.

    According to recent reports, for a long time, frameworks have primarily been designed around how developers write and organize code. Exact suggests another perspective: what if the framework were also designed around how AI agents build, operate, and validate software?

    This approach also reflects a broader movement in the mobile ecosystem.

    Developers increasingly want to share code without necessarily sacrificing platform-specific capabilities.

    Kotlin Multiplatform is an interesting example of this direction.

    Instead of requiring developers to share the entire application interface, KMP allows teams to share business logic, networking, data layers, and other common functionality while maintaining native interfaces using SwiftUI on iOS and Jetpack Compose on Android.

    With Compose Multiplatform, developers can also choose to share the UI itself.

    These approaches demonstrate that cross-platform development doesn't necessarily mean building everything with a single UI framework.

    There are different ways to achieve code reuse, and the best architecture depends on the application and the team's requirements.

    Expo Exact explores another possibility within this evolving landscape.

    Perhaps one of the most interesting aspects of Exact is its approach to AI-assisted development.

    Today, coding agents can generate components, implement features, and refactor existing code.

    But generating code is only part of the development process.

    We still need to run applications, inspect interfaces, interact with components, and validate behavior.

    Exact introduces tooling designed to make these interactions possible.

    This is particularly interesting because it moves beyond AI-assisted code generation.

    It creates an environment where agents can participate in the implementation and validation process.

    As AI becomes increasingly integrated into software development, frameworks designed around these workflows may become more relevant.

    Expo Exact is an experimental project, not a replacement announcement for React Native.

    React Native continues to have a mature ecosystem, extensive library support, and a large community.

    For applications already running in production, migrating to Exact would require significant architectural changes.

    Existing React components, hooks, navigation solutions, native modules, and third-party integrations cannot simply be reused.

    The same consideration applies to other cross-platform technologies.

    According to recent reports, adopting a upcoming framework is not just a matter of changing the runtime. It affects architecture, development workflows, integrations, testing, and long-term maintenance.

    I find Expo Exact particularly interesting because it challenges some assumptions about how cross-platform applications should be built.

    Kotlin Multiplatform has already demonstrated that sharing business logic while preserving native interfaces can be a compelling architectural choice.

    Now, Exact introduces another perspective, combining a latest UI model, a Rust-based runtime, and tooling designed for AI agents.

    I wouldn't consider it a production alternative to React Native today.

    But I would definitely keep an eye on it.

    The future of cross-platform development may not be about finding one framework that replaces all the others.

    It may be about having different architectural approaches for different needs, with AI increasingly becoming part of the development process.

    And that's what makes projects like Expo Exact worth following.

    What do you think about this direction for cross-platform development?

    Estimating Sample Size Before Testing a Law Firm Contact Form

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Law firm clients ask for A/B tests all the time.
    • A few minutes with a sample size estimate before the test starts saves weeks of pointless testing and an awkward conversation later.
    • A standard sample size estimate for comparing two conversion rates needs four numbers:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Law firm clients ask for A/B tests all the time. Shorten the contact form, change the button text, move the phone number. The request is reasonable, but on a typical criminal defense site the traffic to a single page is small, and the number of people who actually submit a form is smaller still. Run a test without checking the math first and you will likely end up calling a winner based on noise.

    A few minutes with a sample size estimate before the test starts saves weeks of pointless testing and an awkward conversation later. This post covers the inputs you need, a short script to do the arithmetic, and what to do when the answer indicates the test is not practical.

    A standard sample size estimate for comparing two conversion rates needs four numbers:.

    Industry observers note that get the baseline from real data. For a contact form, that is form submissions divided by unique visitors to the page over a recent, normal period. If you are not sure the form events are tracked correctly, fix that first. A test built on broken tracking is worse than no test.

    Choose the minimum detectable effect based on what would matter to the firm. A change from 3 percent to 3.1 percent is not worth anyone's time to detect. A change from 3 percent to 4 percent might be.

    The formula for two proportions is short enough to keep in a utility file. This version uses only the Python standard library:.

    With a hypothetical baseline of 3 percent and a target of 4 percent, the estimate comes out near 5,300 visitors per variant, or roughly 10,600 in total. A bigger expected lift, from 3 percent to 6 percent, needs only about 750 per variant. Small differences are expensive to detect.

    According to recent reports, online calculators give similar numbers. The value of the script is that you can drop it into a planning notebook and run it for every page you are asked to test.

    Divide the total by the page's weekly unique visitors. If a charge page gets 400 visitors a week and needs 10,600, the test would run for more than six months. In that time the firm will change other things on the site, search rankings will move and seasonal patterns in arrests will shift traffic. The result would be hard to trust.

    A useful rule: if the estimate runs past eight to ten weeks, the test as designed is not practical for that page.

    You still have choices when traffic is low.

    For the non-technical side of that last option, a write-up on running a conversion test on a low-traffic defense website covers how to initiative and read a test when traffic is thin.

    Sources indicate that on criminal defense sites, many visitors call instead of filling in a form, especially on mobile. If a form change pushes people toward the phone, form submissions fall while total contacts rise. Track calls with a dynamic number or call tracking tool that can attribute calls to the variant, and judge the test on total contacts. Otherwise you can reject a change that actually helped.

    In a recent development, record the baseline, the minimum detectable effect, the sample size, the expected end date and the decision rule in a short document before the test starts. Agree with the firm that you will not stop early because one variant looks ahead after a week. Peeking and stopping early is one of the most common ways small tests produce false winners.

    Sources indicate that when the test ends, report the result with its uncertainty alongside the percentage lift. A firm owner can work with "probably no meaningful difference" as long as they knew in advance that this was a possible outcome.

    More on testing and measurement for law firm websites is gathered in the library on conversion testing for law firm websites.

    Raising alpha above 0.05 shortens tests but makes false positives more likely. Change it only if the firm understands the tradeoff.

    Bayesian methods report results differently, but they do not create information from small samples. Low traffic still means uncertain results.

    According to recent reports, use whichever unit you randomize on, usually consumers. Keep it consistent for the baseline and the test.

    SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It builds websites for defense practices, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

    Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business.
    • It has been revealed that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
    • Industry observers note that an affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing1. What is affiliate marketing? Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!2. What is an affiliate program? An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping? Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands. 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing? Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action. 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices? Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile owners by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.7. Where do I find qualified publishers? The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement? An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases. 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing? Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.10. What is a super affiliate? A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.11. How do we track publisher sales activity? Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard. 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries? Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways: It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business. You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a upcoming audience. It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective. 14. How do I find quality publishers? One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links? Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:A website or blogThrough email marketing and newsletterSocial media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter. Leave a comment on blogs or forums.Write an e-book or other digital product.Youtube 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program? To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.17. What is a commission rate? Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.Who manages your affiliate program? Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.18. What is a cookie? Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration19. How long do cookies last? The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.Final SayingMost new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

    #69413. Tech Report: Lightweight API Clients for Low-Memory Machines

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (769 w)

    Tech Report: Lightweight API Clients for Low-Memory Machines

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that quick answer: On a low-memory machine, the lightest real option is a terminal client such as curl, HTTPie, or xh, followed by a native or Tauri-based desktop GUI.
    • Industry observers note that two clients can show the same request builder and still cost very different amounts of memory.
    • According to recent reports, that baseline is painful in a few common spots: an older 8 GB laptop already running an IDE, browser, and database; a CI container with a hard memory limit that kills a process over the line; a small cloud VM where RAM is billed; or parallel debugging that opens the client against several services at once.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that quick answer: On a low-memory machine, the lightest real option is a terminal client such as curl, HTTPie, or xh, followed by a native or Tauri-based desktop GUI. The popular Electron clients bundle a full Chromium runtime per install and usually hold the largest resident set. Treat every memory figure as something you measure yourself, since idle RAM, a large collection, and several open tabs move the number more than the product name does.

    Industry observers note that two clients can show the same request builder and still cost very different amounts of memory. The difference is usually the runtime underneath. An Electron app ships its own Chromium and Node, then splits work across a main process, a renderer, and a few GPU and utility helpers. That keeps the app consistent across systems, but each helper stays resident at idle, so the baseline is already high before you send one request.

    According to recent reports, that baseline is painful in a few common spots: an older 8 GB laptop already running an IDE, browser, and database; a CI container with a hard memory limit that kills a process over the line; a small cloud VM where RAM is billed; or parallel debugging that opens the client against several services at once. Once the system starts swapping, every tool feels slow, not just the API client.

    Sources indicate that vendor pages rarely publish resident memory, and the numbers shift between releases, so trust only the figure you take on your hardware. Read the process group as a whole, since the main process is one entry and the renderer helpers often hold more.

    Sources indicate that take the reading at three points: after a cold start at idle, after loading your largest real collection, and with five to ten tabs open. Let it settle, repeat twice, and note cold-start time.

    Memory is a range rather than fixed figures, so compare by runtime category and confirm the specific release on your machine.

    It has been revealed that terminal tools win on idle because they exit when the request finishes, with nothing polling in the background. A native or Tauri GUI keeps a window open but uses the system webview instead of shipping a second browser, narrowing the gap while preserving a graphical workflow.

    In a recent development, A terminal client does not hand you a saved collection tree, visual environment manager, or team sync; you rebuild that layer with scripts and Git, which suits some teams and frustrates others. Pick the lightest tool that still runs the assertions and saved scenarios you rely on. If you are weighing a broader move away from your current GUI, the Postman alternatives guide compares tools on more than memory.

    According to recent reports, watch two traps. First, do not read only the main process and miss the renderer and GPU helpers, or you undercount an Electron app by a wide margin. Second, a browser-based or PWA client is not free memory: its tab lives inside the browser, already one of the largest things on the machine. A desktop app such as Powerduck combines an API workspace with code review in one place and sends requests through its local main process, yet on a constrained machine you still measure its resident set the same way rather than assume it fits; one combined window can also replace a separate review tool.

    Are terminal clients really lower on memory than desktop apps? Yes, because they run as one short-lived process with no bundled browser and nothing resident between calls. Saved collections and collaboration then have to come from scripts and version control.

    Does a native or Tauri client always beat an Electron one? It usually has a smaller baseline, but it still uses the system webview, and a large collection or many tabs raise its footprint. Treat the category as a strong hint and confirm with your own measurement.

    Is a browser-based client free memory-wise? No. The tab is charged to the browser, which already holds a large resident set. Closing extra browser tabs often saves more than switching the in-page client.

    Measure the full process group under your largest real workload before you change anything. If the machine is tight, a terminal CLI is the dependable floor, and a native or Tauri GUI is the middle ground when you want a visual workflow. Do not give up assertions just to save memory, and do not tolerate a client that pushes the machine into swapping; the right choice is the lightest one that still catches the failures you care about.

    #69411. Industry News: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (583 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place.
    • Image compression operates on pixel data.
    • Recent findings suggest that JPEG files use marker segments to organize data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place.

    Image compression operates on pixel data. Metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS coordinates — is stored in structurally separate sections of the file. Whether those sections survive compression is entirely a function of how the tool is built.

    Recent findings suggest that JPEG files use marker segments to organize data. The pixel stream starts at the SOS (Start of Scan) marker. Metadata lives in application markers:.

    Low-level libraries like libjpeg and libjpeg-turbo process only the pixel buffer. They do not automatically parse or carry over APPn markers. To preserve metadata, the developer must explicitly intercept markers during reading (via jpeg_save_markers()) and reinject them during writing (via jpeg_write_marker()).

    Sources indicate that metadata behavior varies by library and configuration. Some image libraries strip metadata by default, while others can preserve it when explicitly configured. For example, Sharp removes metadata by default unless preservation options such as keepMetadata(), keepExif(), or keepXmp() are used.

    PNG files store metadata in ancillary chunks:.

    Recent findings suggest that PNG compression itself is lossless — optimizers like OxiPNG reorganize the pixel data more efficiently without changing it. But whether the metadata chunks are preserved depends on the optimizer's implementation.

    WebP uses a RIFF container with dedicated chunks:.

    Sources indicate that IPTC is not part of the WebP specification. When converting from JPEG to WebP, EXIF and XMP can be carried over, but IPTC fields have no standard container in WebP.

    The compression library does not handle it — if the tool wraps libjpeg without marker handling or uses HTMLCanvasElement.toBlob() without separately preserving and reattaching source metadata, the output file will have no metadata regardless of the input.

    Deliberate size optimization — some tools strip metadata to save a few kilobytes per file.

    Format conversion side effects — converting between formats (JPEG → WebP, TIFF → JPEG) can drop metadata fields that the target format does not support.

    Canvas-based workflows operate on decoded pixel data rather than the original file container. Exporting with canvas.toBlob() or canvas.toDataURL() creates a newly encoded image and does not automatically carry over the source file's EXIF, IPTC, or XMP metadata. Applications that need metadata preservation must handle and reattach that metadata separately.

    Recent findings suggest that tools that use WebAssembly-based encoders (MozJPEG, libwebp, OxiPNG) can produce better compression results and can handle metadata if the implementation explicitly copies the relevant sections. The GeoImageTagger Image Compressor uses WASM encoders for compression and is designed to preserve supported metadata as a separate step, including post-compression verification.

    If metadata preservation matters for your pipeline, add a verification step:.

    Recent findings suggest that before compression — inspect the original file's metadata. The Metadata Viewer reveals EXIF, IPTC, XMP, and GPS fields for any supported image.

    It has been revealed that if fields are missing — use a metadata editor to restore them, or switch to a compressor that preserves metadata. The Metadata Editor handles writing EXIF, IPTC, and XMP fields.

    For programmatic workflows, exiftool can copy metadata between files:.

    Metadata preservation is not always the right choice. Personal photos shared publicly may contain GPS coordinates and device information. For privacy-sensitive images, deliberately removing metadata is the correct approach. The EXIF Remover handles selective removal without re-encoding pixels.

    For the full guide, see How to Compress Images Without Losing EXIF, GPS, IPTC or XMP Metadata.

    #69410. Tech Report: How to Start a Side Business While Working Full-Time

    📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2253 w)
