    #69347. For Creamier, Crispier Grilled Cheese, Make It Disneyland-Style

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    For Creamier, Crispier Grilled Cheese, Make It Disneyland-Style

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that is there anything more magical than a visit to Disneyland in sunny, beautiful Anaheim, California?
    • Recent findings suggest that disney actually released the recipe during COVID for its grilled cheese sandwich, which features three different cheeses, as well as a garlic mayo spread for the outside.
    • You might use butter when making your grilled cheeses, but trust us, switching to mayo is the move because it is scientifically disposed to create a more even, crisper crust.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that is there anything more magical than a visit to Disneyland in sunny, beautiful Anaheim, California? While the kids might associate this theme park with their favorite Disney characters or the delightful rides and themed areas, many adults make the pricey trek with an additional consideration in mind: the food. In the theme park where Doritos were first served, one can't-miss creation is the Grilled Cheese Sandwich found at the Jolly Holiday Bakery Cafe (as well as Woody's Lunch Box at Walt Disney World in Florida). If you wanted to replicate its creamy, crispy goodness at home, you might already have the ingredients in your fridge: You'll just need cream cheese for the inside and mayonnaise for the outside.

    Recent findings suggest that disney actually released the recipe during COVID for its grilled cheese sandwich, which features three different cheeses, as well as a garlic mayo spread for the outside. There's cheddar and provolone, but the cream cheese is the star, as it gets oh-so-gooey and decadent when it melts down, and it adds a slight tang that will make your tongue take immediate interest.

    You might use butter when making your grilled cheeses, but trust us, switching to mayo is the move because it is scientifically disposed to create a more even, crisper crust. Think about it: You can spread it easily in an even layer without worrying about tearing the bread, as you might with butter. And the inclusion of garlic is a master stroke that introduces even more flavorful depth to what is, essentially, a simple sandwich.

    Using cream cheese as a filling and mayonnaise as an outer agent of browning is just one way to achieve the grilled cheese of your dreams. While you should absolutely try these two ingredients, we have a few other ideas that can help you achieve the upgraded Disney Parks-inspired sandwich. The first? Cream cheese is just one of three cheeses that go into this toastie; you'll likely use sliced provolone, but at least for the cheddar, you should grate your own. Blocks of cheese that are grated simply melt better than the pre-shredded variety because there are additional ingredients in the latter that help to keep it from clumping, which prohibits it from melting as wonderfully. If you're going to the trouble of including cream cheese to up the gooey-factor, you might as well go full-tilt where the cheddar is concerned. Disney also includes a bit of cream in its cream cheese blend, which will undeniably enhance the richness of the sandwich and keep things gooey for longer. One tablespoon per quarter cup of cream cheese is more than enough.

    To ensure that the sandwich gets its crispiest crust, too, it's notable that you don't drop it into the skillet until the pan is fully heated through(though you can still sprinkle salt onto the pan if you want a little extra seasoning). This is so that the golden outsides can start crisping immediately. At the same time, though, you don't want to have the heat turned up too high — a nice medium to medium-low will do the trick. Any hotter and the outside will burn before the cheese has an opportunity to melt all the way through — not the kind of crispness we're seeking.

    #69343. The Hardest McDonald's Item To Prepare, According To One Former Worker

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (520 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    The Hardest McDonald's Item To Prepare, According To One Former Worker

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There are quite a few challenges, actually, when it comes to working at McDonald's.
    • And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce.
    • In a recent development, peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There are quite a few challenges, actually, when it comes to working at McDonald's. There's a lot of time management involved, as well as customer service and interaction, to say nothing of the physical fatigue from being on your feet for hours. Then there's the actual assembly of the food itself, and while the burger chain with nearly 42,000 locations across the globe has automated many facets of its kitchen, for the most part, employees must still work the machines and put the sandwiches together. So all this begs the question: Is there a menu item that is the hardest to prepare? Food Republic spoke with Tristen Epps-Long, who won Season 22 of "Top Chef" and who is actually a former McDonald's chef, and in his opinion, the dubious honor belongs to the Big Mac.

    His reasoning? "It's multi-layered," he noted. And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce. "It was just a bit more hand work," Epps-Long told us. It seems other McDonald's employees agree with our expert, too, as one person on Reddit reported they had a coworker almost quit after receiving an order for 12 Substantial Macs at once. It is worth noting, though, that Epps-Long did mention that, after a while, Big Macs can lose their undesirable status; you just have to get the hang of making them.

    In a recent development, peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently. It's understandable; the QP is the only McDonald's burger that's cooked fresh, not frozen, so there would be an extra layer of food safety that employees would have to follow in order to prevent cross-contamination with the raw beef product.

    According to recent reports, on the dessert side, the apple pies seem to be a pain to make as well, as one employee on Reddit recounted how the sweet treats take six minutes in the deep fryer, which is apparently long enough to start doing other tasks, but not long enough to finish the tasks before the pies are done. That individual must work at an overseas location as apple pies are baked in the USA. The McFlurries appear to be another annoying menu item to make, likely because the process is so hands-on; unlike the burgers, which get cooked on a timed clam shell grill, employees have to hold the McFlurry cup during every step.

    Now, at the other end of the spectrum, Tristen Epps-Long shared that he found the Egg McMuffin to be one of the easiest things to make, which is slightly surprising, as there are quite a few different elements to it. However, on Reddit, a commenter remarked that the easiest thing for them to make is the plain burgers or cheeseburgers, and this apparently resonated with their peers because the statement has 43 upvotes.

    #69341. Not Ribeye: Bobby Flay Recommends This Steak Cut For The Best Tacos

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (603 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    Not Ribeye: Bobby Flay Recommends This Steak Cut For The Best Tacos

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When taco night rolls around, you'll want to head to the butcher and grab some good meat.
    • Industry observers note that ribeye is America's favorite steak thanks to its rich marbling and tender texture, but you'll rarely find it in taquerias.
    • Unlike ribeye, skirt is cut from the plate primal, a hard-working area near the diaphragm.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When taco night rolls around, you'll want to head to the butcher and grab some good meat. If you're making carne asada, your instinct might be to pick the ribeye. While it might be the gold standard of steak, tacos and ribeye are an inherent mismatch. Tacos are one of the most democratic foods out there, while ribeye is made for deep pockets and expensive tastes. Even Food Network's Bobby Flay recommends skipping it. Instead, he swaps the pricey cut for the seriously underrated skirt steak.

    Industry observers note that ribeye is America's favorite steak thanks to its rich marbling and tender texture, but you'll rarely find it in taquerias. Beyond being pricey, ribeye's assets are its downfall in tacos. In an interview with Food and Wine, Flay revealed the reason why he often chooses to skip ribeye altogether: "[Ribeye] can be inconsistent because the fat doesn't always melt even when cooked properly." This is a real problem in tacos. Encased in a taco, you don't have the option to trim around a rubbery pocket of fat or leave it on the plate. Even if you trim the fat before adding the steak to your tacos, it's so unevenly distributed that you risk ending up with wildly inconsistent slices.

    Unlike ribeye, skirt is cut from the plate primal, a hard-working area near the diaphragm. Rather than being streaked with generous ribbons of fat, it's comprised of long, coarse muscle fibers, which give it a chewier, more fibrous bite along with a bold, beef-forward flavor. Its thin profile may not win it fans at white tablecloth restaurants, but it's exactly why taquerias can't get enough of it. All that surface area compared to its thickness means skirt steak cooks quickly, soaks up marinades fast, and slices evenly, which is everything you want from taco meat.

    There's no cut of beef more well-suited to carne asada than skirt. Literally translating to "grilled meat," the beef is usually marinated in a citrus and garlic blend, with the acidic ingredients helping to tenderize the surface of the meat. After being left to soak up the flavor for a couple of hours, it's then seared or grilled over an open flame or charcoal to impart a smoky, charred flavor (an air fryer also works if you can't grill). Because skirt is such a thin cut, it doesn't enjoy spending too much time over high heat; it only needs around two to four minutes per side. Skirt can be prone to drying out, so it would be wise to avoid cooking past a medium doneness.

    How you cut skirt is just as important as how you cook it. Compared to other cuts, skirt has particularly long, dense muscle fibers, and if you slice them with the grain, you'll leave them intact, resulting in chewy, rubbery bites. Slicing against the grain shortens these fibers, turning them into more satisfying, bite-sized strands. To identify the grain, look closely at the surface of the meat to spot the direction of the muscle fibers running through the beef.

    According to recent reports, although skirt is beloved by taquerias, that doesn't make it suited to all beef tacos. One popular style where we would skip skirt is birria, the slow-cooked, tender beef marinated in a chili-and-spice adobo served with a flavorful broth for dipping. The whole concept of birria revolves around slow-braising, requiring tough, collagen-rich cuts like chuck or beef cheek, which break down into tender, shreddable meat over several hours. While skirt does have some connective tissue, it's simply too thin and lean to survive hours of prolonged heat.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
    • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
    • Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

    Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

    Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

    People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

    Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

    The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

    One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

    The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

    Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

    Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

    Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

    These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

    Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

    The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

    However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

    The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

    Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

    It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

    Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

    The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

    Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

    Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

    People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

    A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

    The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • Recent findings suggest that the perfect burger can be hard to come by.
    • Industry observers note that sometimes, it all comes down to what you mix into the ground beef.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Recent findings suggest that the perfect burger can be hard to come by. When you're going out, Food Republic's list of the best burgers in every state can be helpful, and there are even some great fast food options. But when you're looking for a super juicy and flavorful homemade grilled or pan-fried patty, what's the best route to take?

    Industry observers note that sometimes, it all comes down to what you mix into the ground beef. While Bobby Flay uses only salt and pepper to season his patties, some folks swear by Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder for a kick of flavor. But there's one ingredient you may not have thought of that will keep your end result wonderfully succulent. Try mixing some onion dip into your ground beef. It's one of the clever ingredients that make burgers juicier, and it will add loads of flavor.

    According to recent reports, onion dips generally come seasoned with dried onion and garlic, salt, and other herbs, plus a little sugar for sweetness. Add to that the sour cream base, and you have a rich, bold, slightly tangy, umami-filled burst of flavor that won't overpower your taste buds. And because you're mixing the dip directly into the beef before cooking, it can help keep your patties nice and moist (as long as you don't overcook them). Sour cream is simply cultured cream, so it has a high moisture content, and the added seasonings aren't so coarse that they will burn before the beef itself is cooked.

    In a recent development, when it comes to what dip to use, classics like Dean's French Onion or Daisy Sour Cream French Onion, which is available on Amazon, will work great, but pretty much any brand will work. Depending on how much tangy flavor you want, you'll need about a half-cup to a full cup of dip per 2 pounds of beef.

    The beauty of using onion dip in your burgers is that it's a one-ingredient solution, but you can increase the intensity with extra onion powder or fresh minced or dried onions. Just don't overdo it on the onion pieces, or the patties could fall apart on the grill. If you're going heavy on the amount of dip you use, you may want to think about adding some breadcrumbs as a binding agent. Dried parsley makes a great mix-in, as do other Italian herbs, but you should start sparingly so they don't overpower the flavor you're aiming for.

    According to recent reports, as for toppings, the regular stuff will do, but you might want to hold off on the ketchup and mustard until you've had a bite. Caramelized onions are an obvious choice, or you can give your burger some crunch with crispy fried onions. And you can always add an extra dollop of onion dip on top for more creamy flavor and texture.

    Sources indicate that lastly, this trick will also work with a dried dip mix. Just mix it in with sour cream before you make the burgers. And if you want a similarly juicy bite without the added zing, try using mayonnaise in your burger. But for a juicy texture and plenty of zesty flavor, grab that onion dip out of the fridge.

    Who Makes Costco's Kirkland Signature Red Blend Wine?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (429 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola.
    • In a recent development, A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend.
    • DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola. Yet one unknown that perpetually probes consumers is which producer is behind Costco's private-label alcohol. The Kirkland Signature labels conceal a treasure trove of well-priced bottles, spanning not only every major liquor style, but also a varied selection of wine and (formerly) beer.

    In a recent development, A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend. This vino comes packaged in an eye-catching 1.5-liter bottle, all while sold for under $10. You'd think that such a size would make sleuthing the producer tricky. However, the brand behind this budget pick is listed directly on the bottle: DC Flynt MW Selections. A large tech giant responsible for both cellaring and bottling, this producer and distributor oversees a widespread U.S. and global portfolio, making it a natural match for Costco.

    DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California. This suggests that at least some of the grapes are assembled in California's Central Valley region, as Modesto is only about two hours from Napa Valley — although precise vineyard sourcing is unknown. The same brand is also behind bottles from Sonoma, Napa, and Alexander Valley. Similarly, it produces Kirkland Signature's chardonnay as well.

    Recent findings suggest that as one of the least expensive Kirkland Signature wines, you might not expect an oenophile-appreciated experience with this bottle. Yet despite this accessible price point, the wine garners positive reviews: "A proof that [mass-marketed] wines can actually be good," noted Vivino reviewer Anton A., who gave the wine 4 stars. On the platform, the wine is rated 3.7 out of 5 stars, with over 3,500 reviews. Furthermore, other reviewers have given it favorable scores, praising the wine's balance of fruit-forward and spice flavors.

    Typically, affordable California red blends are known for sweet "jammy" flavors, meaning the composition is heavy on sugar. Yet as noted right on the Kirkland label itself, this bottling strays from aggressive fruit-forwardness. Notes of oak and spice help contrast the fruit, a sentiment upheld by reviewers: "More [Bordeaux-like] than a California fruit bomb, but extremely tasty," noted another Vivino user — although some drinkers do take problem with its moderate palate. "[Not] flavorful enough, not jammy enough, not [oaky] enough," critiqued a Reddit user. Still, at a price point that even beats out affordable Trader Joe's picks, it's wine worth adding to a Costco shopping haul.

    Forget Mayo: Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad (Hint: It's Egg Free)

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy.
    • Industry observers note that toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify.
    • But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy. But if you like a bit of garlic in yours, then toum — a Lebanese spread as rich in flavor as it is in fluffiness — is the answer you've been looking for.

    Industry observers note that toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify. Far lighter in texture than mayonnaise but not quite as airy as whipped cream, it's a perfect middle ground that imparts serious flavor to fish. While it won't have quite the same richness as mayonnaise, since it lacks eggs, this can actually work in your favor. It gives your final product a lighter flavor profile that's highly conducive to other simple ways to level up tuna salad, such as adding horseradish or capers. It's perfect for when you want a protein-laden lunch that doesn't feel too heavy and won't leave you in need of a nap.

    Served cold, it's delicious. But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else. The pungent notes fill your nostrils and blend with cheeses and toasted bread to create something as satisfying as any cheeseburger. Just be careful not to let any fall out, as toum's oil-based emulsion can separate or scorch when exposed to excessive heat.

    If you like a denser tuna salad, one packed with hearty chunks and thick vegetables, then mixing in a dollop of toum and calling it a day works just fine. However, if you want something quite light and creamy, almost like a tonnato sauce, then you need some high-powered beating action. By adding the toum and tuna to a stand mixer or a bowl with an electric hand mixer, you shred the fish into fine pieces. This allows the fluffy nature of the garlic spread to almost suspend the protein, giving the illusion of increased volume without actually adding any additional ingredients.

    Recent findings suggest that toum can be quite acidic depending on the brand and recipe, and the lemon juice can rapidly work with any pickles or relish to make your tuna salad a bit overpowering. To avoid anything too intense, you may want to switch to sweeter varieties. Still, if you're a diehard believer in acidic additions, apples, hot honey (a true kitchen multitasker), or a pinch of sugar can all help balance acidity quite well and add little nuances of their own that work well with garlic.

    #69325. What It Means When You Hear A Cowbell Ring At McDonald's

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (614 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    What It Means When You Hear A Cowbell Ring At McDonald's

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that mcDonald's is one of the biggest chains in the world, so being curious about what goes on behind the scenes is only natural.
    • To get to the bottom of this, Food Republic reached out to sisters Melissa Montes Blanco and Kristina Montes, third-generation owners and operators of several McDonald's locations.
    • Sources indicate that as of writing, the Quarter Pounder is McDonald's only burger made with fresh, never-frozen beef.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that mcDonald's is one of the biggest chains in the world, so being curious about what goes on behind the scenes is only natural. People love to throw around wild theories (no, the chicken nuggets aren't made from pink slime), but there are plenty of factual goings-on that might surprise fans. For instance, many customers are shocked to learn that McDonald's cooks aren't flipping your patties, or that every time you order a Quarter Pounder, you're setting off a cowbell in the kitchen.

    To get to the bottom of this, Food Republic reached out to sisters Melissa Montes Blanco and Kristina Montes, third-generation owners and operators of several McDonald's locations. According to them, the cowbell rings because the Quarter Pounder is cooked to order. "When you go through the [drive-thru] or [order] delivery, whenever the order comes in, we will hear a cowbell in the kitchen, and that signals to the team to drop the meat at that point," they explained.

    Sources indicate that as of writing, the Quarter Pounder is McDonald's only burger made with fresh, never-frozen beef. When preparing meat for the Major Mac or cheeseburger, the frozen patties are batch-cooked and left in heated holding cabinets, so they can be assembled in seconds. The Quarter Pounder is a slightly more involved process, so when a customer places an order, the crew needs to be ready to throw a patty on the grill. It doesn't help that the patty takes much longer to cook. According to McDonald's, a regular patty takes around 42 seconds on the grill, while a Quarter Pounder patty nearly triples that at 112 seconds (almost two minutes). Fast food is in the name, so speed is everything, and a cowbell is a pretty effective way to spring the crew into action. The Montes sisters went on to explain that this extra time may be why you're sometimes asked to pull forward and wait outside of the drive-thru queue.

    It has been revealed that mcDonald's has the inner workings of the fast food game down to a science, from sensors that alert employees when a car pulls into the drive-thru to smart weight-checking scales for delivery orders that compare the total weight of the bag against expected targets to flag missing items before it leaves the kitchen. Most of its stores operated like a well-oiled machine long before the fresh-beef Quarter Pounder was introduced in 2018, so are the cowbells really necessary? According to several employees, they're nothing more than a nuisance.

    It has been revealed that the alarm is part of McDonald's Kitchen Video System (KVS), which functions as a replacement for paper tickets by showing orders on screen for the crew. Alerts have traditionally been beeps and buzzes, so employees were caught off guard when a cowbell joined the mix. After the latest grill display was installed, one self-identified employee took to Reddit to share their candid thoughts, claiming that "[it was] driving virtually everyone bats." They added, "It plays [an] unbelievably grating and repetitive cowbell sample instead of something more to the point ... It's annoying as hell[,] and nobody likes it except for a single manager. I thought about doing everyone a favor and just unplugging the speakers." A quick scroll through the replies was enough to show that this employee was far from alone, with plenty of coworkers piling on to share their own cowbell horror stories.

    Despite waves of employee complaints, the cowbells don't seem to be going anywhere. McDonald's hasn't publicly responded to the backlash, and a November 2026 TikTok from McDonald's franchisee and content creator McBossladi has those all-too-familiar cowbells ringing in the background.

    #69322. The Best Chain Restaurant Grilled Reuben Melt, According To Customers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (421 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Chain Restaurant Grilled Reuben Melt, According To Customers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that it's hard to mess up a Reuben because the ingredients are so simple: corned beef, sliced thin, tangy sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Thousand Island dressing (or Russian), all of which are sandwiched between two pieces of sturdy rye bread.
    • To that end, Food Republic did the legwork and created a list of the top Reubens you can order from a chain, from customers' perspectives, and one of the entries actually comes from Culver's.
    • Sources indicate that were you aware that Culver's even had a Grilled Reuben Melt on its menu?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that it's hard to mess up a Reuben because the ingredients are so simple: corned beef, sliced thin, tangy sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Thousand Island dressing (or Russian), all of which are sandwiched between two pieces of sturdy rye bread. No matter where you get your Reuben from, it's safe to say there are typically no bad ones — just good, better, and best.

    To that end, Food Republic did the legwork and created a list of the top Reubens you can order from a chain, from customers' perspectives, and one of the entries actually comes from Culver's. The Midwestern favorite, better known for its unique ButterBurgers, apparently makes the best grilled version of the sandwich you can find.

    Sources indicate that were you aware that Culver's even had a Grilled Reuben Melt on its menu? Because for as many customers who sing its praises, there appear to be an equal number who didn't even know it was an option. But what an option it is; it's a classic version, with lightly toasted bread, piles of salty corned beef, and melty Swiss cheese made in Culver's home state of Wisconsin.

    One Reddit user shouted out the sandwich, writing that it "matches or beats some of the ones that I've had at many diners." Another commenter remarked that Culver's "slaps in general[,] but this goes hard for a fast food Reuben." Meanwhile, yet another Redditor called it "the best thing on the menu and the best [Reuben] I've ever had.".

    One of the best things about Culver's menu is how customizable it is, and the Reuben is no different. Culver's maintains a fairly long list of toppings that you can add to your melt; one Reddit user claimed that "[grilled onions] and mushrooms are the easiest way to elevate the sandwiches," though keep in mind that you might have to request customizations in person because online ordering doesn't always have the option. You could also add raw onions for a sharper bite, lettuce for a little greenery, tomato for some extra umami flavor, and, for a small fee, some thick-cut bacon.

    Another user suggested adding a burger patty to the sandwich, calling the addition "incredible." Finally, if you're not a huge fan of rye, you could also swap it out for sourdough (the melt would then actually more closely resemble the best non-traditional chain restaurant Reuben, found at Schlotzsky's Deli), or opt for its Kaiser bun, brioche roll, gluten-free bun if you have a wheat allergy.

    #69318. 12 Powdered Gravy Mixes, Ranked Worst To Best

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3021 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    12 Powdered Gravy Mixes, Ranked Worst To Best

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • It has been revealed that as most pro home chefs will tell you, making gravy from scratch isn't exactly rocket science.
    • Even so, the kind of store-bought gravy mix you choose matters — after all, anything you're planning to drown your meat and taters in had better be good.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    It has been revealed that as most pro home chefs will tell you, making gravy from scratch isn't exactly rocket science. With the help of a little flour, butter, and broth, you could be on your way to a delicious gravy in just a few minutes. Still, there may be times when you simply aren't feeling up to it — whether you've had a rough week or are drowning in to-dos, packets of powdered gravy mix can prove a simple, flavorful fix.

    Even so, the kind of store-bought gravy mix you choose matters — after all, anything you're planning to drown your meat and taters in had better be good. That's why I decided to make it my mission to test some of the most popular powdered gravy options in my area in hopes of offering my honest opinion about which truly deserves a spot in your kitchen.

    Industry observers note that in the upcoming post, I'm giving a complete rundown of every store-bought powdered gravy mix I could find, including the pricing, size, and taste of each. Bear in mind that the details mentioned in this article are subject to change and that the gravy packet selection featured here may not be reflective of what's available in your area. With that, join me as I prepare, taste, and rank 12 store-bought powdered gravy mixes from worst to best.

    Prices are as of the date of publication and may vary based on region.

    Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is a no-frills Walmart-branded product that is, surprisingly, one of the costlier options on the list when you consider its price per unit. Though tagged at only 92 cents per packet, each pack contains .87 ounces, meaning you'll pay roughly $1.06 per ounce of powdered gravy.

    It has been revealed that great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is prepared using the standard 1 cup of water per 1 packet of mix, and its ingredients include monosodium glutamate (otherwise known as "MSG"), which may pose a problem for gravy lovers who may be sensitive to the ingredient. I tore open the packet, and its unappetizing, artificial smell hit me right away. Once cooked, the mixture turned creamy and thick, but its color seemed unnatural, especially when compared to homemade. I gave it a hesitant taste, and nope, not good — Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix tasted like stale chicken and literally made me gag.

    Would I recommend purchasing Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix? No way. Not only does its bright yellow color not resemble any chicken gravy I've ever made, but the taste was barely tolerable. I'm sure you could try improving this store-bought gravy with Worcestershire sauce, but I say, if it's convenience you seek, there are other options more deserving of your coin than this one.

    I hate to have to rank yet another Great Value powdered gravy mix so close to the bottom of the list, but it simply cannot be helped. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix is a bit cheaper than its chicken-flavored counterpart — expect to pay 78 cents per .87 ounces, which works out to around 89.7 cents per ounce of powdered gravy. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix doesn't contain the MSG that the chicken flavor includes, but that doesn't mean I recommend purchasing it — like the former, it has a weird smell and taste that I simply can't get past.

    I prepared Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix according to the package directions and watched it bubble and simmer on the stove. The mix eventually turned the typical light brown color normally associated with turkey gravy and had an uber-thick consistency. I let it cool slightly before giving it a quick taste — sadly, it had the same stomach-churning qualities as the previous flavor. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix tasted woefully artificial; in fact, the additives or chemicals present in the gravy were just about the only thing I could taste. Needless to say, I would never dish up Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix to guests at Thanksgiving — you'd be better off leaving not-so-Great Value picks like this one on the shelf.

    Before offering my opinion here, I have to be honest and say I'm not a person who prepares peppered gravy often. That mentioned, I'm willing to bet Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix doesn't quite encapsulate its classic flavor the way other options do.

    According to recent reports, southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix costs $1.22 per 2.75 ounces, with a unit price of 44.4 cents per ounce. As is typical for many peppered gravy mixes on the market, this packet contains a little more powdered gravy mix per pack than other varieties and flavors. Its preparation requires more water, too — you'll need 1 ¾ cups this time around versus the usual 1 cup.

    According to recent reports, southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix tasted annoyingly bland, with a flavor very similar to what you'd get if you added black pepper to plain cream. Though thick, it had no richness of flavor, and I couldn't imagine it doing much to elevate anyone's sausage gravy. I flipped the packet over and was surprised by what I saw on the ingredient list: Palm oil and modified food starch were the first ingredients mentioned, which is hardly a good way to start a high-quality gravy, if you ask me. As I said, I am by no means an expert in peppered gravy, but based on first impressions alone, I'd say skip this brand and opt for other, richer, more flavorful brands on the market.

    Recent findings suggest that if you're surprised to see McCormick Brown Gravy Mix ranked lower on the list, join the club. I, for one, adore brown gravy, and with McCormick being one of the most popular gravy and seasoning brands on the market, I figured I'd be in for a real treat. Expect to pay 97 cents for .87 ounces of it, making each ounce cost roughly $1.12.

    When cooking up McCormick Brown Gravy Mix, I couldn't help but feel excited — its texture was thick and glossy, and the gravy had a deep brown hue that just screamed umami beef. It even had the savory, enticing aroma of a succulent pot roast, so imagine my surprise when I discovered the gravy tastes, quite literally, like nothing.

    Recent findings suggest that that's right — McCormick Brown Gravy Mix features a flavor so weak I could barely taste anything at all. To think McCormick Brown Gravy Mix smelled and looked so great without delivering flavor even half of what was teased is mind-boggling. Needless to say, McCormick Brown Gravy Mix isn't worth the buy — I'd recommend picking up some beef broth and making your own simple brown gravy or choosing one of the higher-ranking varieties over this one.

    Recent findings suggest that though not the best out there, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix is a dark horse in terms of taste and performance. The gravy comes sold in an .87-ounce pack and was priced at 83 cents, about 95 cents per ounce. It contains artificial ingredients along with a host of additives, but hey, if that kinda stuff doesn't bother you, feel free to ignore those stats.

    I went into my tasting of Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix with low expectations — almost every Amazon Grocery item I've sampled in the past left me underwhelmed. Much to my amazement, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix held its own in terms of consistency and aroma — it was a bit thinner than a few other options on the list, yes, but still managed to be just thick enough. I also found its glossy deep brown appearance mesmerizing, and its smell rich and meaty, just the way a good brown gravy should be.

    According to recent reports, going in for a slurp, I didn't walk away disappointed — though the flavor was nowhere near as potent as its aroma, it was leaps and bounds better than McCormick. I could clearly taste its beefy notes, and its umami depth was decent overall. One thing I will say is that Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix tastes slightly watered down; still, I think it will get you by if you're looking for a tasty, inexpensive brown gravy to crown your mashers.

    Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix is pretty good; though not a peppered gravy kinda gal, I have an appreciation for this brand and would recommend it over Southeastern Mills any day. This mix comes in a 2.75-ounce packet, only this time, you'll need to add 2 cups of water instead of the 1 ¾ cups Southeastern Mills requires. Each packet costs $1.33, meaning you'll cop this powdered peppered gravy for about 48.4 cents per ounce.

    According to recent reports, when cooking up Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix, the first thing I noticed was its golden hue. The yellowish tinge of the Pioneer-branded gravy made it more attractive than the stark white presentation of Southeastern Mills. It was just as thick as the former brand, if not thicker, though whether or not its flavor would prove better was yet to be seen.

    Industry observers note that so, how'd Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix taste? Though I still consider its flavor mundane compared to traditional chicken or brown gravies, Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix had more depth than Southeastern Mills. It's not listed in the ingredients, but there seemed to be a hint of butter flavor in the mixture — this deepened the taste and added complexity. All in all, if I were to grab a packet of peppered gravy for breakfast, this is the brand I'd get — not only does it look better, but its taste is pretty decent, too.

    Recent findings suggest that mcCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix wasn't too bad — it isn't something I'd choose over homemade gravy for Thanksgiving dinner, but it's good if you're in a pinch and want something cheap. The gravy comes sold in a .87-ounce packet for $1.63, and while this might not sound super expensive, it's actually a little pricier than others, at $1.87 per ounce.

    McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix yields a light brown color I found fitting for turkey gravy — it certainly looked the part, featuring a medium-thick consistency and glossy appearance. McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix has a poultry-like flavor that's pleasing but leans more chicken than turkey in my opinion. Nevertheless, I consider this turkey gravy option to be one of the punchier, more robust picks out there, and though I don't necessarily consider it holiday worthy, it might be good to have a packet or two in your pantry for days when you're low on time.

    It has been revealed that fire & Smoke Society Massive Sunday Brown Gravy Mix is a super unique option, and though I probably wouldn't buy it again, you might consider trying it if you're looking to sample something outside of the norm. The packaging here has the kind of aesthetic that makes you think it's fancy by looks alone — its price also stands out, at $1.72 per 1-ounce pack, working out to $1.72 per ounce. A quick scan of the ingredients reveals several surprises — though not a clean ingredient pick by any means, some additions — like cumin, chili powder, and even coffee — left me curious as to what kind of flavor I was in for.

    I prepared the gravy as per its 1 cup to 1 packet instructions and immediately noticed a difference in its texture compared to the others. Fire & Smoke Society Major Sunday Brown Gravy Mix yields a thinner, silkier texture than most. Its aroma was totally unexpected, as it was more akin to grill spices than savory beef. After tasting Fire & Smoke Society's Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix, I found myself torn — the taste wasn't gross, but didn't encompass the type of flavor I expect from a classic brown gravy.

    It has been revealed that is Fire & Smoke Society Significant Sunday Brown Gravy Mix good? Yes! Would I buy it again? Probably not. Blame it on my traditional taste buds, but for me, this powdered gravy mix is just OK.

    According to recent reports, is there a difference between country and peppered gravy? Apparently, there is, and as it stands, I prefer the former. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was a breath of fresh air flavor-wise, but I suppose that isn't surprising given I love practically anything that the Kinder brand produces. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was priced at $1.72 per 1.9 ounces at my local Walmart, working out to about 90.5 cents per ounce.

    In a recent development, kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was truly phenomenal in terms of taste and texture. First and foremost, the gravy recommends preparing it with 2 cups of milk, which automatically gave it a richer, sweeter finish. Once cooked, the gravy was thick and featured a stark white appearance flecked with tons of contrasting black pepper throughout.

    Recent findings suggest that kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning tastes almost identical to creamy, buttery, garlicky mashed potatoes, no spuds needed. I'd imagine this would taste incredible paired with creamy taters, and I wouldn't hesitate to dish it up as a turkey topper during the holidays. As if things couldn't get better, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning uses fairly clean ingredients, with nowhere near as much of the ick featured in other powdered gravy mixes on the list. With all things considered, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning is one of my favorite powdered gravy mixes on the market.

    Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix costs $1.72 for .85 ounces making it one of the most expensive powdered gravy mixes on the market at $2.02 per ounce. It's the only gluten-free organic chicken option on the list, and I honestly didn't expect it to taste as good as it did. Not that I have anything against organic foods — I actually love them and find the use of minimal ingredients refreshing. Still, in the world of gravy, I guess I just didn't expect a natural option like this one to hold its own when pitted against others containing various flavor-boosting additives. Thankfully, this humble pick from Simply Organic proved me wrong.

    Simply Organic chicken gravy calls for the standard 1 cup of gravy packet seasoning per 1 cup of water. As it cooked, it began to take on a sauce-like consistency that was thick, glossy, and light brown. I gave it a taste and was floored — this organic pick boasted a flavor way better than any other store-bought chicken gravy I've tried.

    It has been revealed that simply Organic chicken gravy had a bold, savory, and garlicky flavor beautifully enhanced with prominent notes of celery seed. Thus, though expensive, you can rest assured that your money is going to good use — Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix is a phenomenal replacement for homemade when you don't feel like whipping up chicken gravy on your own.

    Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is the only organic brown gravy on the list, and let me tell you, it did not disappoint. Unlike its chicken-flavored predecessor, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is slightly cheaper, at 1 ounce for $1.72 ( $1.72 per ounce). Being the organic grab that it is, expect Simply Organic brown gravy to be non-GMO and free of artificial colors, flavors, and ingredients. One of its best attributes is its use of cornstarch rather than flour, as this makes it a great option for people looking to ditch wheat.

    According to recent reports, I was delighted to find Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix packing so much flavor — after the previous brown gravy duds, I didn't have much hope that there was a truly good packaged option out there. In truth, Simply Organic's brown gravy is one of the most flavorful in its class — it was one of the few to truly capture the beefy, oniony savor I come to expect from a good homemade brown gravy.

    It has been revealed that one thing to note is that Simply Organic brown gravy has a medium consistency and a color a lot lighter than others in its category. Still, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix would make the perfect companion to roast beef or over creamy mashed potatoes, and I doubt anyone would be able to detect the difference between it and homemade.

    In a recent development, yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is unlike any other gravy I've tried — I had never sampled jalapeño gravy before, nor did I know it existed. Now that it's on my radar, in my cabinet it will stay. It's really that good, even if it is $2.50 per 2.82-ounce packet (89 cents per ounce)!

    Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy contains no artificial flavors, which to me is pretty impressive. Though not gluten-free like the aforementioned Simply Organic picks, it does at least contain fewer additives while still managing to achieve unbelievably thick results. You only need to use 2 cups of water per packet to cash in on this irresistibly luscious golden gravy; its texture was so rich and smooth my mouth watered just at the sight of it.

    In a recent development, aside from its tantalizing consistency, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy tastes incredible — I'd describe its flavor as similar to high-quality jalapeño nacho cheese, but with less emphasis on the cheese. It's quite spicy, and though not unbearably so, still isn't something I'd recommend offering to kids. All in all, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is an amazing option I'd buy over and over again — try it on fried chicken cutlets, potatoes, stuffing, or hot sandwiches. Yum!

    The 12 powdered gravy mixes selected for this article were chosen based on availability in my area, with most sourced from Walmart and Amazon. Each gravy mix was ranked primarily based on texture and flavor, although other factors, like ingredients and pricing, were considered. As always, pricing and availability are subject to change.

However, instead of serving the expected pie this year, opt for this cheesecake — in addition to a creamy base full of intense pumpkin flavor, the whole dessert is topped with pecans and a generous drizzle of caramel sauce.

    A two-pack of Ferrara's Bakery 8-inch Pumpkin Cheesecake with Caramel and Pecan Topping is available at Costco for $119.99.

This bready cake is incredibly versatile and can be the foundation for many fall recipes. For an elegant touch, it's topped with silk cherry blossoms, and comes in a striking box tied with a beautiful ribbon, too. If you're not a fan of nuts or raisins, this cake is free of both, so nothing gets in the way of the spiced carrot flavor.

    The Cake Bake Shop 8-inch Round Carrot Cake is available at Costco for $159.99.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, mcDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu. Alongside familiar faves, you'll find items Americans can't order, the most envy-inducing among them arguably being the Egg BLT McMuffin. Once you hear what's in it, don't be surprised if you catch yourself planning a trip to our northern neighbor.

    It has been revealed that the Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin. A second version uses nearly identical ingredients but swaps the whole leaves for shredded lettuce. You can only get this variation at McDonald's restaurants located inside Walmart stores — part of a decades-old partnership that once placed roughly 1,000 outposts in the retail chain. McDonald's later closed hundreds of them as drive-thrus became the main source of sales, though Walmart continues to host many locations in Canada.

    According to recent reports, to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative. Your best bet is to start with a Bacon, Egg & Cheese McMuffin, which already ticks off half the ingredients. Ask for a touch of mayo, which gets you close to the sauce of the Canadian original. Since lettuce and tomatoes are lunchtime items, your odds improve near the end of breakfast hours when stores are prepping the lunch menu — you'll likely have to order them at the counter or window.

    The Egg BLT might have already convinced you to add McDonald's to your itinerary next time you're in Canada, but it's not the only breakfast item worth the detour. One that caught our eye was the Mighty McGriddles. While the U.S. offers the Bacon, Egg & Cheese and Sausage, Egg & Cheese varieties separately, the Canadian version puts both to shame by stacking a double helping of hickory-smoked bacon, a sausage patty, egg, and cheese between two maple-flavored griddle cakes — a gloriously overstuffed creation that lives up to its name. The Mighty McMuffin follows the same logic, coming loaded with both meats for anyone who can never decide between the two.

    Industry observers note that another familiar face on Canadian McDonald's breakfast menus is the bagel, though while America only offers plain, Canada also serves sesame and everything varieties. You can even order one toasted with butter or Philadelphia cream cheese — widely known as the best store-bought brand — as if you're at a proper bagel shop.

    According to recent reports, canada's McDonald's restaurants aren't afraid to put a twist on U.S. staples, and they also introduce new items altogether. You won't find chicken anywhere on the standard U.S. breakfast menu, which makes the Chicken McGriddles feel like a curveball up north. The simple yet delicious sandwich pairs a breaded chicken patty with two sweet, maple-flavored griddle cakes for some serious sweet-and-savory fusion.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Org ↗ Open Full Page

    The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (466 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
    • Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
    • Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

    Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

    Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

    Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

    They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

    The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

    Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

    The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

    The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

    Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

    Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

    By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

    The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

    The water group also revealed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

    Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

    Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, mentioned:.

    “It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

    The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

    In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

    However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

    The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

    The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

We all know about croissants, and, yes, when infused with the right sweet elements, they definitely count as a dessert, but that's just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to French desserts. In fact, there is a seemingly never-ending list of eye-catching sweet treats that hail from the country. The ones found below, though, are so mouthwateringly delicious that everyone should try them at least once in their lives.

    It has been revealed that if you aren't already familiar with French desserts, it doesn't matter if you are fluent in the language or not; the names of the country's culinary creations don't always alert you to what they actually are. With this in mind, if you're interested in sampling a few — why wouldn't you be? — but aren't sure where to start, we can help point you in the right direction. So, get your fork and spoon ready, because once you learn about the collection of French desserts below, you'll be dying to get your hands on them.

    The tart Tatin may have a fancy name, but don't let that fool you. It is actually akin to an apple pie, just flipped upside down — and there's nothing extravagant about that. The French version of the dessert also has humble origins. As the story goes, in the late 1800s, Caroline (of Caroline and Stephanie Tatin's Inn, located south of Paris) forgot to put a crust on the bottom of her apple pie. Due to being exceptionally busy, she decided to put it on top instead and see what would happen. When she took it out of the oven and flipped it over, she saw that her misstep led to a happy result: The apples were beautifully caramelized. When she served it to the inn's guests, it was an immediate success, and the tarte Tatin was officially born.

    Creating a tart Tatin is fairly accessible to novice home cooks. It only calls for five ingredients: apples, flour, butter, eggs, and sugar. The trickiest part is arranging the slices of fruit in a decorative way on the bottom of the pan. Actually, despite her massive culinary repertoire, Ina Garten admits it is the recipe she makes most because it is not only delicious, but easy to create, as well. If it's good enough for Garten to come back time and time again, you'd better believe it's a French dessert everyone should give a go at least once.

    Crème brûlée is one of the most easily recognizable and widely popular French desserts in the United States, but, interestingly enough, its origins are somewhat disputed. France, England, and Spain all claim to be the birthplace of the dessert. Regardless, since its invention, wherever that happened to be, there's no doubt it has fully integrated itself into traditional French cuisine, and if you've never had the joy of eating one before, you are truly missing out.

    Sources indicate that in its most basic format, crème brûlée is made with just four ingredients: egg yolks, sugar, heavy cream, and vanilla bean. While simple, the elements come together to form a creamy, custardy delight. Then, the top is scorched to form a layer of burnt sugar that's to die for. Topping it with a couple of fresh berries is also customary, but either way, it is simplicity at its finest. In fact, this is one case where the sum is much greater than its parts. In addition to the sweet, rich flavor of the custard itself, part of the fun of eating one is using a spoon to crack the burnt layer on top. It not only adds a caramelized taste but contributes textural variation, and that is always a plus. Whether you decide to try your hand at making crème brûlée yourself or choose to seek it out from a restaurant, it's a French dessert that's worth your attention.

    Éclairs have been around since the 1860s, and today, they are one of the more popular French desserts found in the United States. For good reason, too; they are tasty enough to go down in a flash. Speaking of which, the word directly translates to lightning.

    According to recent reports, name and popularity aside, éclairs are made with choux pastry, which is similar to doughnut pastry, but devoid of baking soda, baking powder, and yeast, and relies on steam to rise. As a result, after being formed into long cylindrical pieces, the dough cooks up to be exceptionally light and airy. That's just the start of the legendary éclair, though. They are also filled with pastry cream or custard and then topped with either fondant or ganache icing — both of which are harder styles of icing, so you can still feel free to enjoy éclairs with your hands.

    According to recent reports, arguably, the most popular flavor of éclair is chocolate, but thanks to the versatility of the choux pastry shell, they are welcoming to a world of other flavors as well. Everything from caramel to pistachio to Nutella to strawberry to matcha with chocolate and beyond can be found enhancing the delightful little pastry.

    It has been revealed that french yogurt cake, or gâteaux au yaourt in the native language, is another easy yet extremely satisfying dessert that deserves some time in the spotlight. In France, it is a popular recipe for kids to learn, likely because of the simple recipe, which calls for three eggs, one part oil, one part yogurt, two parts sugar, three parts flour, and leavening. Even so, when it comes out of the oven, you have a drool-worthy, slightly tangy cake that is moister than pound cake (if you can fathom that) while still presenting a delicate crumb.

    Since French yogurt cake is not a common restaurant offering, if you want to give it a taste, you'll likely have to make one yourself. Or, at the very least, enlist a friend to do it — um, mom? Thankfully, though, it is one of the more straightforward must-try French desserts out there, so it should be attainable for even the most novice home cooks. The simplicity of the French yogurt cake also makes it prime for a plethora of flavor infusions. So, if you want to add citrus, or brandy, or fruit to the mix, go right ahead.

    Crêpes are a delicately thin pancake-like creation that's ready and waiting for a world of flavor and ingredient infusions. Still, a Crêpes Suzette is quite possibly the most delicious and famous version of them all. It consists of classic crêpes in a sauce made of sugar, orange juice, and an orange liqueur, like Gran Marnier. The entire thing is also smothered in brandy and set on fire, which leads to a caramelized, citrusy, sweet flambé sauce that will draw just about anyone in. Heck, even watching a chef prepare one catches the eye, and that's why it's often done in full view when ordered in a restaurant.

    Interestingly enough, crêpes Suzette is another iconic French dessert that was first created by accident — and this particular story is not disputed. In 1895, Henri Carpentier, a 14-year-old assistant waiter at the Maitre at Monte Carlo's Cafe Paris, was preparing dessert for the Prince of Wales (who'd later become King Edward VII of England). While doing so, he accidentally caught the cordials he was working with on fire, and instead of becoming flustered and starting over from scratch, he tasted the sauce and realized he'd come up with something extraordinary.

    Don't let the flambé scare you too much if you want to try creating one at home; it truly does lead to exceptional flavor. However, you can still make a tasty rendition sans the potential fire hazard; it just won't be quite as authentic.

    First and foremost, Mont Blanc is known for being the highest mountain in the Alps. However, for those in the know, it is also a delectable French sweet treat with Alpine-inspired appeal. In fact, when created, the Mont Blanc dessert resembles a snow-capped mountain peak, so the name is more than fitting. The exact origins of it is uncertain, but a reigning theory is that it was developed in Paris, France, in the 19th century. During that era, chestnuts started to grow in popularity in the region, and people began incorporating them into sweet dishes, instead of the customary savory ones.

    Sources indicate that the main components of a Mont Blanc dessert are as follows: It starts with a crisp meringue base, which is topped with thin strands of chestnut purée, and then finished off with a pile of whipped cream. Traditionally, a vermicelli tip is used to pipe the chestnut puree, but other shapes are also common. Either way, though, the yummy chestnut puree is the star of the show, offering a nutty, rich flavor that offsets the creamy whipped cream and meringue in a delightful way.

    In a recent development, hailing from the Basque region in southwest France, the Gâteau Basque became widely popular in the 19th century. Its growth in the culinary scene is largely attributed to a particular baker, Marianne Hirigoyen, who first sold them in local markets before opening a brick-and-mortar bakery. Since then, the gâteau Basque's acceptance into French culinary tradition has been more than cemented. Actually, fast-forward to today, and there's now a museum and a two-day festival in October dedicated to the dessert. If that doesn't tell you exactly why it is a must-try French recipe, we don't know what would.

    Whether you call them canelé, cannelé de Bordeaux, or canelé Bordelais, these yummy little French pastries are time-consuming to make — the dough needs to rest for up to 24 hours before baking. Even so, their delectable mix of textures and delicious buttery, custard-y flavors are worth the effort used to make them and then some.

    According to recent reports, small and cylindrical with fluted edges, the center of canelés are made with flour, milk, sugar, butter, vanilla bean, eggs, salt, and rum. Once mixed with care, the dough rests for an extended time before baking in copper molds. After they're cooked, a delicious coating of edible beeswax and butter fills the molds and is also poured over the top before baking again. When that's done, you're left with delicious bite-sized (well, almost) custard-filled cakes featuring a caramelized crust on the exterior. Considering miniature copper fluted molds are not a customary tool in most homes, canelés aren't the first dessert we recommend trying to make at home. However, if you ever see them in a French bakery or restaurant, you'd be a fool not to give them a try.

    According to recent reports, opera cake is one of the coffee desserts that are always worth ordering, and guess what? It's also a French dessert everyone should try at least once. That is, of course, if you know what's good for you — and in this case, we truly hope you do.

    Industry observers note that created by Cyrique Gavillon, the opera cake is just as much a thing of beauty as it is a delectable flavor wonderland. A rectangular-shaped cake at heart, it is made with alternating layers of coffee syrup-soaked almond cake, buttercream, and ganache, and then topped with a rich dark chocolate icing. Once completed, it not only looks stunning, but provides your palate with a mix of nutty, chocolatey, creamy, rich, coffee flavors that are hard to beat. Yes, it sounds a whole lot like tiramisu when the elements are taken at face value, but it is a delightful dessert all its own when it comes to how the ingredients come together. Plus, it's French, not Italian. Just saying.

    According to recent reports, while simple to make, the Île flottante presents itself as an elegant dish, and as such, is a mainstay in French cuisine. In fact, while it's remarked French people prefer to purchase dessert from a local bakery, it is one recipe many natives still have in their repertoire. It just so happened to be Julia Child's favorite old-school dessert, as well. Since she is credited with bringing French cuisine to the United States and helping it grow in popularity, following her lead regarding the greatest culinary hits of the country just makes sense.

    Recent findings suggest that similar to éclairs, which we've already discussed, profiteroles are made with hollowed-out choux pastry, filled with custard or cream, and topped with icing. What sets them apart is their shape. Instead of being long and cylindrical, profiteroles are formed into small bite-sized balls. As a result, they are the perfect sweet treat for bringing to a gathering or munching on if you simply want a few bites. However, once you get a taste of their scrumptious textures and flavors, trying to eat just one will be quite a complicated task.

    It has been revealed that again, like éclairs, the most common icing flavor for profiteroles is chocolate. Still, they come in a myriad of other flavors, as well, so they have what it takes to pique the interest of many. For example, if chocolate is too one-dimensional for you — we are judging you — you can also make chocolate hazelnut profiteroles, vanilla ones, or just about any other flavor you can dream up.

    In a recent development, last but certainly not least on our list of French desserts you need to try is clafoutis. The name may sound posh, but it's actually another sweet treat that's incredibly easy to make, so you don't have to be an established French baker to create one at home. Plus, it may be a dessert, but it is also acceptable to eat it for breakfast. Okay, now we are really listening.

    Clafoutis consists of fruit smothered with a thick custard made from sugar, flour, milk, and eggs. The texture is akin to flan, but undeniably has all the French flair a Francophile could want. Most traditionally, cherries create the meaty fruit of clafoutis, but other berries and fruits, like raspberries, are also commonly used to pull off the recipe. While not necessarily a dessert, if you want to go in a savory direction, fruit can also be substituted for prosciutto, cheese, and tomatoes, so think of it like a choose-your-own-adventure type dish. No matter how you build it, though, clafoutis is one French creation that deserves more recognition, at least in the States.

    #69300. Forget Butter Or Mayo: Spread This Rich Ingredient On Bread For Heartier Grilled Cheese

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (451 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

    Forget Butter Or Mayo: Spread This Rich Ingredient On Bread For Heartier Grilled Cheese

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A grilled cheese is already plenty hearty, but the common tip of using cured meats to increase its satisfying flavor — like in this tasty maple bacon variation — may interfere with your filling's texture if you prefer a smooth, gooey filling.
    • Industry observers note that duck fat is one of the most prized cooking fats in the culinary world because it has a higher smoke point than butter (around 375 degrees Fahrenheit) and a beautifully silky texture rich in subtle, meaty flavors.
    • Using duck fat on grilled cheese is pretty easy, but there are a few tricks that can really maximize your results.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A grilled cheese is already plenty hearty, but the common tip of using cured meats to increase its satisfying flavor — like in this tasty maple bacon variation — may interfere with your filling's texture if you prefer a smooth, gooey filling. Duck fat is the perfect way around this because it adds meatiness without changing any other ingredients, enriching the bread with umami with just a single smear.

    Industry observers note that duck fat is one of the most prized cooking fats in the culinary world because it has a higher smoke point than butter (around 375 degrees Fahrenheit) and a beautifully silky texture rich in subtle, meaty flavors. Just like spreading it on burger buns, using duck fat on grilled cheese can give you crispier bread because you can cook it at a higher temperature. When left at room temperature, it has a consistency similar to softened butter, making it easy to spread or drop in a pan, depending on your preference. Its unique composition of fats and subtle meaty flavor mean you'll notice its richness even in small amounts. Though it has a touch of gaminess, it's quite subtle and serves to elevate creamy and aged cheeses alike with an added layer of complexity.

    Using duck fat on grilled cheese is pretty easy, but there are a few tricks that can really maximize your results. Blending it with another fat, using it for some added seasoning, and picking the right pan can all give you the perfect sandwich.

    Mixing a fat with a high smoke point with one that burns more easily is a simple way to combine the best of both worlds. The richness of butter is irreplaceable, but you can incorporate some of duck fat's higher-heat cooking properties by swirling the two together before spreading the mix on your bread. Similarly, you can also bring your duck fat to a low, gentle simmer and add herbs and aromatics to flavor it beforehand. Whether you do this when rendering the fat yourself or just for a few minutes before adding your sandwich, a bit of sage can lend tremendous depth, while a smashed clove of garlic can mimic the rich flavor of toum.

    Industry observers note that while a nonstick pan is great for butter since it doesn't retain as much heat, you might want to go in the opposite direction for duck fat. A heavy cast iron or stainless steel skillet helps prevent the surface temperature from dropping when you add the sandwich, maintaining that lovely heat that makes duck fat work so well. Plus, animal fats are great for cast iron's seasoning, helping you maintain your pan's coating while you cook!
